publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract The National Weather Service (NWS) recently developed an AI-powered neural machine translation system to deliver potentially life-saving weather warnings to the 68.8 million Americans who speak a language other than English at home. This forum piece makes the case that applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have a vital and largely untapped role in the continued development of this technology. First, dialect and register variation across multilingual groups demands ongoing sociolinguistic attention, as translation differences affect how people understand and conceptualize risk. Second, the metrics NWS uses to evaluate translation quality leave communicative effectiveness unmeasured, and demographic categories used to identify target audiences miss the breadth of bilingual experience, both of which applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have the tools to address. Third, indigenous, oral-tradition, and signed languages present challenges that corpus-based training cannot resolve alone, and reaching these groups will take community linguistic fieldwork and delivery beyond text. Warnings are only as effective as their comprehension, and applied linguistics can increase understanding and action during extreme weather events across a multilingual nation.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
record.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines strategic content licensing between a generative artificial intelligence (AI) platform and a digital news publisher in digital news markets, an important issue for understanding where AI platforms rely on publisher content while competing for user attention. It analyzes how citation intensity shapes licensing incentives, pricing, user diversion and welfare. Design/methodology/approach We develop a game-theoretic model of two-dimensional horizontal differentiation in which the AI platform has a comparative advantage in content integration and the publisher has a comparative advantage in factual accuracy. The model examines how citation intensity, hallucination risk, user preference correlation and per-use royalty jointly determine equilibrium outcomes. Findings Licensing between AI platforms and publishers arises from a trade-off between two countervailing forces: entry displacement and engagement expansion. Content licensing requires sufficiently high citation intensity; mutual gains additionally require low preference correlation. The pricing effects of citation intensity are nonmonotonic. Subscription prices can rise or fall depending on the strength of citation relative to royalty costs. User diversion is shaped by the balance between referral traffic expansion and direct substitution. Welfare improves only when engagement expansion dominates entry displacement. Originality/value This study models AI–publisher licensing in a two-dimensional Hotelling framework of asymmetric comparative advantages, conceptualizing citation intensity as a content-composition variable that shapes output quality, user traffic and royalty payments beyond existing display-level constructs.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to develop an explainable deep learning framework for forecasting tail risk and volatility in cryptocurrency markets, with a particular focus on differences between energy-intensive and ESG-oriented digital assets. It aims to assess how volatility dynamics and downside risk exposure vary across environmental profiles and market regimes and how these differences can inform risk-aware investment decisions. Design/methodology/approach The proposed framework uses a quantile long short-term memory model to estimate predictive quantiles and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), enabling the modeling of asymmetric, fat-tailed and regime-dependent risks. The analysis focuses on four cryptocurrencies – Bitcoin and Litecoin (energy-intensive) and Algorand and Chia (lower-energy alternatives). The model integrates SHapley Additive exPlanations-based explainability and a regime classification (calm vs stress). Robustness is assessed using 20-, 40- and 60-day rolling evaluation windows, while predictive performance is evaluated through coverage rates, hit ratios and Kupiec and Christoffersen back testing procedures. Findings The results reveal substantial heterogeneity across the four cryptocurrencies rather than a uniform green-versus-energy-intensive ranking. Chia records the lowest Q50 root mean squared error (0.00149) and mean absolute error (MAE) (0.00119), whereas Algorand has the lowest full-sample CVaR (0.0293) and Litecoin the highest (0.0411). Regime results are also asymmetric: Bitcoin’s Q10 violation rate rises from 8.74% in calm periods to 11.74% in stress periods, while Litecoin and Algorand record more Q10 violations in calm than in stress regimes. Chia combines the lowest global Q10 violation frequency (2.98%) with the highest mean CVaR violation loss (0.127419), showing that infrequent breaches can still be severe. These findings support asset-specific tail-risk monitoring and cautious use of energy-profile information in risk-aware investment decisions. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by integrating quantile-based deep learning, explainable artificial intelligence, regime-specific diagnostics and sustainability considerations into a unified risk-forecasting framework. Its main value lies in complementing connectedness and spillover studies with interpretable, asset-level distributional forecasts and formal tail-risk backtesting. The results provide decision-support information for risk monitoring and portfolio analysis, but do not imply that lower-energy cryptocurrencies are universally safer or that the observed differences are causal.

record.title: The AI engagement paradox: algorithmic congruence and its inverted-U effect on tourist experience quality

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management
record.abstract_text: Purpose Despite widespread adoption of AI agents in restaurant and gastronomic tourism settings across Asia, practitioners consistently observe a counterintuitive pattern: increasing AI service involvement initially enhances but subsequently undermines tourist experience quality. This study aims to term this the “AI engagement paradox” and introduce algorithmic hospitality congruence (AHC), a new second-order construct to theorise and empirically confirm the inverted-U relationship between AI congruence and gastronomic tourist experience quality (GTEQ). Design/methodology/approach A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design was used across three Asian markets (Hong Kong, Singapore, Bangkok). Phase 1 comprised 24 semi-structured interviews using the critical incident technique to develop AHC construct items. Phase 2 involved a quantitative survey (N = 412). AHC was grounded in cognitive load theory (CLT). Polynomial regression with response surface methodology confirmed the inverted-U effect; partial least squares structural equation modelling validated the construct. Common-method-bias mitigation and endogeneity-robustness checks used temporal separation, Harman’s single-factor test with a marker variable and Gaussian copula endogeneity correction. Findings AHC comprising culinary AI precision (CAP), emotional service resonance and cultural contextual fit (CCF) demonstrated robust construct and discriminant validity. AHC exhibited a significant inverted-U effect on GTEQ. Cultural collectivism steepened the negative slope, while digital literacy shifted the tipping point rightward. Research limitations/implications This study delivers empirically grounded deployment guidance for hospitality operators in AI-integrated gastronomic settings. The validated 15-item AHC scale provides a diagnostic instrument for monitoring AI-experience alignment. Operators are advised to benchmark their AHC composite score against the estimated tipping-point zone (4.18–5.04 on a seven-point scale), differentiate deployment intensity by tourist digital literacy, apply conservative ceiling margins for high-collectivist segments and treat CCF as a foundational design requirement rather than a localisation afterthought. Digital literacy investment is reframed as a direct hospitality revenue strategy. Originality/value This is among the first studies to theorise and empirically confirm an inverted-U effect of AI congruence in gastronomic tourism. AHC is rigorously differentiated from five related constructs and grounded in CLT from the outset. The findings challenge the linear AI benefit assumption dominant in hospitality AI research and provide indicative deployment guidance for practitioners.

record.venue: The International Journal of Information and Learning Technology
record.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transformed into research value within Southeast Asian universities by investigating the institutional and adaptive mechanisms linking technological capability to perceived research excellence and technology commercialization success. Design/methodology/approach Drawing upon institutional theory and dynamic capability theory, the study develops the Institutionally Regulated Research Adaptability framework and tests it using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Data were collected from 2,371 respondents across 170 universities in eleven Southeast Asian countries, with institutional-level aggregation supported through within-group agreement and interclass correlation diagnostics. Findings The results demonstrate that institutional AI regulatory capacity exerts stronger effects on adaptive academic reconfiguration than foundational technological capability conditions. Dynamic research agility emerged as the strongest predictor of perceived research value realization. The proposed negative moderating effect of excessive regulatory readiness was not supported; instead, regulatory structures reinforced adaptive responsiveness. Importance–performance map analysis further identified dynamic research agility and regulatory-ethical framework readiness as the most critical strategic intervention priorities. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, while institutional aggregation may mask within-university variation. Future research should employ longitudinal designs and comparative multi-group analyses to examine national-level institutional heterogeneity across higher education systems. Practical implications Universities should prioritize institutional AI governance maturity, strengthen adaptive research agility, and strategically align faculty capability development with regulatory frameworks to translate AI capability into sustainable research and commercialization outcomes. Social implications The study highlights how institutionally coordinated AI integration can strengthen regional research ecosystems, support responsible digital transformation, and enhance Southeast Asia's academic innovation capacity within emerging knowledge economies. Originality/value This study advances AI-in-higher-education scholarship by shifting analytical focus from technology adoption to institutionally coordinated value transformation. It introduces institutionally regulated research adaptability as a novel explanatory mechanism and provides one of the first large-scale multilevel empirical examinations of GenAI-enabled research transformation across Southeast Asian higher education systems.

record.abstract_text: Purpose This paper aims to reframe board gender diversity as a strategic governance capability rather than a symbolic initiative or universal performance lever. It explains inconsistent diversity–performance findings and clarifies when diversity may strengthen oversight in algorithmically mediated environments. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on structured evidence mapping and interdisciplinary research in corporate governance, leadership, efficiency economics, organizational demography and artificial intelligence (AI) governance, the paper develops a structured integrative conceptual synthesis focused on power, expertise–authority alignment and technological oversight. Findings Diversity effects are contingent rather than automatic. Board gender diversity is most likely to strengthen governance when three enabling conditions are present: representation thresholds that convert presence into voice, expertise aligned with authority and inclusive power structures that enable challenge. Under algorithmic complexity, these conditions may strengthen oversight of bias, explainability, privacy, cybersecurity, vendor dependence and technocratic capture. Practical implications Boards and policymakers should move beyond numerical representation to structural influence. Diverse directors should occupy consequential committees, have relevant expertise and decision rights and be supported by practices that enable challenge. Boards should evaluate participation, committee assignments and technology-governance structures so diversity contributes to accountability, risk oversight and resilience rather than symbolic compliance. Social implications Representation-focused reforms are insufficient when formal inclusion does not produce influence. More substantively inclusive governance can strengthen accountability and stakeholder responsiveness in algorithmic organizational environments. Originality/value The paper moves beyond the business-case debate by integrating intersectionality, governance, efficiency and AI-governance perspectives into a mechanism-based framework showing how board diversity becomes a strategic governance capability under algorithmic complexity.

record.title: Designing transparency in AI influencer marketing: a consumer–agency architecture

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Purpose The purpose of this study is to develop an understanding of AI influencer transparency and its effects on affective and cognitive trust, engagement and consumer well-being. Design/methodology/approach This paper presents a conceptual synthesis of influencer marketing, consumer psychology and human–algorithm interaction research. Findings This paper introduces the Consumer–Agency Architecture (CAA) framework, distinguishing between information, control and provenance transparency. CAA posits that effects of transparency on consumer outcomes are driven by reductions in reactance, whether affective or cognitive. Information transparency primarily mitigates affective reactance; control transparency reduces cognitive reactance; and provenance transparency can attenuate both. Lower reactance, in turn, can support the formation of affective and cognitive trust, engagement and consumer well-being. The framework further identifies boundary conditions that either strengthen or weaken the relationship between transparency and reactance. Research limitations/implications This paper proposes a conceptual framework that remains to be empirically tested. It also posits that transparency effects in AI influencer marketing are primarily driven by reactance, not gains in perceived authenticity. The developed model also assumes that transparency forms have distinct rather than additive or even nonlinear effects on cognitive and affective reactance. Such assumptions could be tested in future work. Practical implications Brands and platforms should treat transparency as a portfolio of design levers rather than a single disclosure: match the specific type of transparency to the focal objective, anticipate trade-offs and avoid one-size-fits-all transparency that can erode trust. Social implications CAA provides a consumer-welfare lens for governing AI-influencer ecosystems by clarifying how transparency can support consumer agency. Originality/value CAA frames transparency in AI-influencer marketing as a means of respecting and protecting consumer agency, offering a mechanism-based foundation for designing ethically grounded, trust-sustaining AI-mediated brand relationships.

record.venue: Journal of Entrepreneurship in Emerging Economies
record.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) is associated with changes in entrepreneurship education in emerging economies, focusing on entrepreneurial competencies, student cognition, venture originality and early graduate behavior. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a multisource, multicohort quasi-experimental design. Principal analyses draw on an approximately 900-student longitudinal survey and a preliminary 18-month graduate follow-up. Published evidence on educator perspectives and on 150 business plans with 45 interviews across three Chinese universities is used only for contextual triangulation and is not pooled with the study-specific statistical analyses. Findings In the principal student analyses, generative AI was associated with stronger opportunity recognition but lower divergent thinking and higher confirmation bias. Predictive analytics was associated with more evidence-based evaluation, while structured intelligent tutoring was associated with stronger metacognitive reflection. Published business-plan evidence is used only to contextualize homogenization. The 18-month venture-creation differences were not statistically significant and remain exploratory. Research limitations/implications The nonrandomized design, incomplete wave-specific attrition information, unavailable matching diagnostics, reliance on published contextual evidence for homogenization and educator perspectives and short follow-up period limit causal claims and cross-context generalization. Future studies should use controlled designs, complete longitudinal reporting, longer graduate tracking and cross-country comparisons. Practical implications Educators should require prompt logs, independent evidence checks, revision rationales and originality rubrics that reward local validation, assumption testing, judgment and distinctive venture logic. Social implications In emerging economies, AI can broaden access to entrepreneurial feedback and market knowledge, but inadequate guidance may yield generic ventures detached from local needs. Originality/value The study extends entrepreneurship education ecosystem thinking by treating AI as an active mediator of cognition and venture artifact production whose educational role depends on tool function, assessment design and institutional governance.

record.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) digital humans, developed to mimic humans, have emerged as promoters in marketing. Although existing studies have identified that AI digital humans' anthropomorphism shapes marketing outcomes, the multidimensionality of anthropomorphism remains underexplored. Focusing on historical figure-inspired AI digital humans in tourism destination marketing, this study examines how their multiple anthropomorphic features influence consumers' responses under the Computers are Social Actors and Media are Social Actors paradigms. Design/methodology/approach An online survey (N = 435) was conducted in 2026. Respondents completed a questionnaire after watching a typical travel vlog featuring a historical figure-based AI digital human. Findings We revealed that voice, behavior and mental anthropomorphism influence consumers' parasocial interactions with AI digital humans, which subsequently affect consumers' attitudes toward tourism destinations. Mental anthropomorphism mediates appearance, voice and behavior anthropomorphism's effects on parasocial interactions. Furthermore, mental anthropomorphism's effect is conditioned by consumers' familiarity with the AI digital human's historical figure prototype. Research limitations/implications This study extends existing research by demonstrating that AI digital humans' multiple anthropomorphic features shape consumers' parasocial interactions, with historical figure familiarity serving as a moderator. However, nonprobability sampling and a single cultural context restrict generalizability, warranting cross-cultural research with probability sampling in the future. Practical implications This study provides practical insight into developing AI digital humans in tourism marketing. Marketers should systematically optimize their human-likeness across voice, behavioral and mental traits, while considering consumers' individual differences. Originality/value This study fills the research gap in AI digital humans by unpacking the multidimensionality of anthropomorphism and showing that its effects are contingent on consumers' traits.

record.abstract_text: Purpose While organizational knowledge conversion (OKC) is central to value creation, its translation into individual employee performance remains insufficiently understood, particularly in artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled contexts where knowledge is abundant but must be appropriately adapted and ethically applied to generate meaningful outcomes. Data were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling in AMOS for measurement model, hierarchical regression and Hayes’ PROCESS macro to test mediation and moderated-mediation effects. Findings The results show that OKC significantly enhances employees’ job efficiency, effectiveness and quality. CKU partially mediates these relationships, indicating that knowledge should be adapted to task-specific contexts for greater performance outcomes. Furthermore, EAIC strengthens the indirect effects of OKC on performance via CKU, suggesting that ethical norms surrounding AI use enhance responsible and effective knowledge application. Originality/value This study extends the knowledge-based view and socialization, externalization, combination and internalization model by linking knowledge conversion to individual-level performance outcomes. record.abstract_text: Purpose Current research on AI-enabled manufacturing transformation largely focuses on the firm-level dimensions of R&D, production or marketing, with few studies examining how AI drives manufacturing transformation at the ecosystem level. This study addresses this gap by investigating the AI-enabled reshaping paths of manufacturing firm innovation ecosystems (MFIE) from a dynamic capability perspective. Design/methodology/approach This multi-case study adopts a dynamic capability perspective to conduct comparative analysis of four typical manufacturing firms, with data triangulated from in-depth interviews, corporate archives and industry reports, thereby identifying both common patterns and differentiated paths of AI-enabled MFIE reshaping. Findings The reshaping path comprises three components: differentiated reshaping pressures as the trigger, AI-enabled dynamic capability construction as the mediator and inter-ecosystem coopetitive replacement as the outcome. At different reshaping stages, focal firms build AI-enabled opportunity identification, solution diffusion and standard locking capabilities to resolve corresponding pressures. Four distinct paths are identified: technology efficiency enhancement, emerging market expansion, independent R&D technology breakthrough and ecosystem platform dominance. Different AI application strategy combinations lead to heterogeneous dynamic capability effects, influencing reshaping outcomes. Originality/value Departing from the single-ecosystem evolution perspective, this study conceptualizes MFIE reshaping as coopetitive replacement between old and new ecosystems and constructs a dynamic capability-based path framework and classification matrix. The study provides actionable guidance for managers to select and implement reshaping paths and offers implications for industrial policy formulation.

record.venue: ACM Transactions on Computing for Healthcare
record.abstract_text: Connected health integrates sensors, mobile devices, and information technology to realize the real-time collection and transmission of medical data, providing patients with more personalized and efficient medical services. In this context, medical image segmentation technology plays a vital role as a key digital medicine tool in connected health. However, its effective deployment across diverse clinical settings and data sources remains challenging due to inherent variations in imaging modalities, patient demographics, and device characteristics. Currently, connected health requires highly efficient AI models for real-world medical applications. The versatility of the model across diverse environments is of great significance. Domain Generalization (DG) has emerged as a crucial solution to address these challenges of connected health. Previous work focuses on the domain similarity calculation on the final layer output of the backbone model, which ignores the impact of the multi-scale features. In this article, we proposed a Domain Pyramid Attention Network (DPANet), which aims to transfer knowledge from source domains to unseen domains for medical image segmentation at a multi-scale level. The overarching goal is to enhance the efficiency of connected health systems through this innovative knowledge transfer mechanism. DPANet is capable of learning multi-scale similarity between two kinds of domains through a Domain Similarity Pyramid Attention Module (DSPAM). We also designed Domain Prototypes (DP), which can enhance the flexibility of the knowledge pre-extracted from source domains for better transferability. A simple fusion method is adopted to merge the multi-scale features for the final segmentation prediction. DPANet is evaluated on Brain Tumor segmentation and Retina Fundus segmentation tasks, achieving an average Dice improvement of 1.14% and 0.98% on these two tasks, respectively.

record.abstract_text: While large language models (LLMs) have captured global attention for their linguistic abilities, our work harnesses their power to overcome traditional barriers in querying Linked Data (LD) and Resource Description Framework (RDF) triplestores. This article presents an innovative framework that integrates LLMs into conversational user interfaces (UIs), enabling the dynamic generation of precise SPARQL queries without the necessity for constant retraining. Most conversational UI models struggle with adaptability as they require frequent retraining whenever datasets are updated or expanded. This limitation impedes their effectiveness as general-purpose extraction tools. To address this challenge, our approach 1 seamlessly incorporates LLMs into the conversational UI process, fostering a more sophisticated understanding and interpretation of user queries and enhancing overall responsiveness. By leveraging the advanced natural language processing capabilities of LLMs, our method improves RDF entity extraction in web systems that utilise conventional chatbots. Furthermore, it extends the functionality of these chatbots, allowing them to respond directly to queries based on the RDF schema while providing an assistive interface that deepens understanding of the dataset and its underlying domain. This facilitates the extraction of more meaningful information. By adopting this approach, interactions become more refined and context-sensitive, a crucial advancement for managing the intricate query structures commonly found in RDF datasets and Linked Open Data (LOD) endpoints. We have evaluated our approach in practical settings by assessing the tool’s ability to address complex queries and to answer general ecological queries, with the outputs evaluated by human experts. The results demonstrate a notable improvement in system expressiveness and response accuracy, showcasing the potential of LLMs to transform information retrieval. The findings not only confirm their adaptability in enhancing existing systems but also open up exciting possibilities for their deployment in specialised web information domains, paving the way for future research in this evolving field.

record.abstract_text: AI-generated review summaries are reshaping how consumers access product information, but their influence also extends to consumers who write reviews. Examining Amazon’s rollout of AI-generated review summaries, we find that these summaries encourage more review contributions and richer content. Consumers discuss product attributes absent from the summaries and elaborate on topics already covered. A controlled experiment suggests that summaries strengthen consumers’ belief that their contributions, together with others’, help future buyers make informed decisions. The increase in review contributions is stronger for products with many existing reviews or mixed ratings. Platform managers could prioritize summaries for products with mixed ratings, for which additional reviews can provide a more complete picture for future buyers. To build on richer review content, platforms could use writing prompts that highlight product attributes underrepresented in AI summaries. However, additional analyses suggest that AI summaries disproportionately benefit products that already sell well, potentially reinforcing sales concentration. Platforms could increase exposure for niche or new products, whereas policymakers could encourage fairness standards and periodic assessments of how AI-generated summaries affect product visibility and sales concentration. These findings highlight the potential of AI summaries to encourage consumer contributions, drawing attention to the risk of increased sales concentration.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Purpose This exploratory study examines how two conversation-based AI models, ChatGPT (USA) and DeepSeek (China), frame fundamental political concepts, “freedom, equality, democracy, social order” and the role of the state within political communication. It aims to compare the normative priorities and ideological assumptions in their responses and assess their possible relationship with the geopolitical contexts of their development. Design/methodology/approach The research used a structured comparative design and qualitative content analysis. Findings Both models generally use similar democratic discourses when explaining freedom, equality, and democracy, but differ in value prioritization. ChatGPT foregrounds individual autonomy, personal rights, and democratic processes, whereas DeepSeek emphasizes collective welfare, social harmony, and the state's responsibility to maintain social order. Practical implications The study highlights the importance for policymakers, technology developers, and media professionals of understanding ideological asymmetries in AI-mediated political communication, and stresses transparency and critical awareness in conversational AI systems. Social implications The implicit normative assumptions of conversational AI can influence political information acquisition, democratic discourse, and cross-cultural understanding. Their spread in everyday information environments may shape how users interpret political concepts in unseen ways. Originality/value The study treats generative AI not merely as a technological tool but as systems situated in different geopolitical contexts that can participate in shaping social-political discourse. Comparing ChatGPT and DeepSeek offers an empirical framework for assessing ideological positioning and normative differences in conversational AI.

record.abstract_text: Although artificial intelligence (AI)-driven digital twins (DTs) are increasingly promoted for sustainable built asset management, there is limited empirical evidence of their full lifecycle application – particularly in emerging economy contexts that combine technical, environmental, and human-centric performance indicators. This study examines the integration of an AI-enabled DT system across the design, construction, and operational stages of ‘Nirmitee Tower’, a green-certified commercial complex developed by a mid-sized construction firm in Central India. Adopting a mixed-methods case study approach, the research collected triangulated evidence from system analytics, environmental performance metrics, semi-structured interviews, and post-occupancy surveys. Operational definitions were applied for key measures such as material waste, comfort score, and heating, ventilation, and air conditioning energy use, with baselines drawn from comparable pre-DT projects. Key findings include: a 21% reduction in project delivery time, a 35.9% decrease in material waste, a 28.3% reduction in annual energy use, a 21.1% reduction in water consumption, and a 32% improvement in occupant comfort scores. This study contributes by providing a validated, multi-dimensional assessment framework for AI–DT performance, by demonstrating a rare emerging market case of full lifecycle DT integration in a small- and medium-scale enterprise context, and by aligning technical results with UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, and 13).

record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming both personal and professional life. In this exploratory study, we investigate the potential role of AI in psychotherapy, focusing on systemic family therapy. We designed a simulation in which psychotherapists interacted with ChatGPT in a role-play scenario involving a distressed couple with a young child. Post-session interviews were held to assess participants’ perceptions of empathy, authenticity, risks, and professional implications. Our findings reveal that while AI can simulate empathy and facilitate useful reflection, it lacks the embodied relational presence crucial to therapy. In this article, we first discuss these results in relation to relevant literature on psychotherapy, technology, and AI. We then introduce a theoretical discussion, drawing on Bowen’s theory of emotional triangles, to speculate about the potential of new, implicit or explicit “technosocial triangles” among humans, therapists, and AIs. While this is a hypothesis rather than an empirical conclusion of our study, we argue that Bowen’s framework helps us imagine how AI might reshape relational systems in families and therapy.

record.abstract_text: Background/Objectives: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurological disorder that adversely affects cognition, memory, and overall quality of life. Identifying AD in its initial phase is especially challenging when patients display cognitive impairments. Conventional methods rely on physicians to manually examine patients and analyze images, which is time-consuming and prone to errors. This review examines the use of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques for diagnosing AD using CT scans and MRI brain imaging. Methods: Research papers published from 2018 to 2026 were sourced from Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and Semantic Scholar. The techniques that were investigated in this study include Convolutional Neural Networks, 3D Convolutional Neural Networks, transfer learning, Vision Transformers, ensemble models, and multimodal approaches. Five research questions were posed to analyse the practicality of using AI-driven techniques in clinical settings, their novelty, scalability, robustness, and accuracy. Results: This study found that AI models can autonomously extract information from brain images and yield highly accurate results, with numerous researches demonstrating over 90% accuracy. Deep learning applied to MRI imaging is effective, while CT-based techniques can detect brain alterations when MRI is inaccessible. Different data types, including imaging, age, medical history, and vocal characteristics, can provide valuable insights into AD. However, issues remain, such as dataset discrepancies, variations among scanners and individuals, and insufficient testing of complex models on diverse populations. Conclusions: Future efforts should focus on accurate and transparent AI, integration of multiple data types, rapid and secure models, and testing on large datasets from multiple hospitals. AI should be developed to assist physicians in accurately diagnosing AD rather than replacing them.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Microplastic pollution requires rapid and reproducible monitoring methods that can complement labor-intensive visual and spectroscopic analyses. This study develops a morphology-aware artificial-intelligence framework for automated classification of field-collected microplastic particles and diatom algae in optical microscopy images. A public freshwater dataset containing 1,140 images from four classes (algae, filament, fragment, and pellet) was analyzed. After image-quality auditing, 1,137 unique images were retained for morphology–texture analysis, while deep-learning experiments used the original image collection under a fixed train/validation/test protocol. Handcrafted morphology and texture descriptors were evaluated with Random Forest, Extra Trees, radial-basis-function Support Vector Machine, and Histogram Gradient Boosting. Histogram Gradient Boosting achieved a cross-validation macro-F1 of 0.9341 ± 0.0255 and a held-out test accuracy of 0.9342. Deep-learning experiments compared ResNet50, Swin Transformer, and a CNN–Transformer fusion model combining ResNet50 and Swin representations. The fusion model achieved an accuracy of 0.9240, macro-F1 of 0.9222, and macro-AUC of 0.9954 on the 171-image test subset. Class-wise AUCs were 1.0000, 0.9950, 0.9886, and 0.9982 for algae, filament, fragment, and pellet, respectively. The results show that morphology-aware machine learning and complementary CNN–Transformer representations can support automated freshwater microplastic screening and provide a reproducible basis for environmental monitoring workflows.

record.title: Information Overload and Disutility in Generative AI Systems as Cognitive Extension: A Bounded Rationality Perspective

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI systems promise cognitive extensions by enhancing information access and use. However, from the bounded rationality perspective, their utility is fundamentally constrained by inherent human cognitive limitations. This article argues that when the volume of AI-generated information exceeds users’ processing capacity governed by working memory constraints, attentional resources, and verification capabilities, it produces cognitive disutility rather than enhancement. We introduced a formal model to quantify this interaction, demonstrating that net cognitive benefits decline systematically as information overload increases beyond individual processing thresholds. The analysis reveals that successful cognitive extension depends not on maximizing informational output but on strategically aligning AI design with human cognitive ergonomics and individual differences in processing capacity. Ultimately, truly augmentative systems must minimize cognitive overhead to prevent overload, while preserving users' epistemic agency and decision-making autonomy.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical training, but evidence from African residency programs is scarce. We assessed how internal medicine residents in Ethiopia use GenAI and how they perceive its impact on clinical learning and clinical decision-making. Methods We conducted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study consisting of a national cross-sectional online survey of internal medicine residents (June to August 2026), followed by two focus group discussions (FGDs) with 10 residents at two universities (September 2026) to explain the survey findings. Perceived impact was measured with five-point Likert items and two composite scores (learning, five items; decision-making, eight items). Associations with frequency of use were tested with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. FGD data were organized deductively into categories based on the survey topics. Results Of 252 respondents from 18 institutions, 98.8% had used GenAI and 75.4% used it daily; ChatGPT was used by 91.6% of users. The mean composite score for perceived impact on clinical learning was 3.83 out of 5 (70.7% high) and for clinical decision-making 3.86 out of 5 (67.7% high). Agreement was highest for improved differential diagnosis (90.8%), learning efficiency (81.9%) and support for self-directed learning (79.5%), and lowest for ward-round performance (64.3%) and confidence in complex cases (71.4%). Daily use was more frequent among residents with more than three hours of daily internet use (82.3% versus 66.7% to 67.4%; p = 0.024) and was not associated with age, sex, marital status, year of residency, device access or formal training. In the FGDs, residents described GenAI as a fast, supportive tool for learning and clinical work, as an aid to reasoning and not a replacement for physician judgment, and as a possible threat to independent learning. Conclusions Residents perceive GenAI as helpful for self-directed learning and diagnostic reasoning while keeping final responsibility for clinical decisions. These findings reflect perceptions and not measured outcomes, so objective evaluation of its effects on learning and clinical performance is needed.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Sustained cognitive engagement, short and mistimed sleep, chronic stress and reduced recovery co-occur in AI-intensive environments, yet how this profile acts on brain energy metabolism is unknown. We built a neuron–astrocyte genome-scale model of human grey matter from Human-GEM v2.1.1, contextualised each cell with human single-nucleus expression, made transport, sodium-pumping and glutathione-recycling costs explicit, and calibrated one parameter to measured cerebral glucose use. Without further fitting the model reproduced the astrocytic share of oxidative metabolism measured by ¹³C spectroscopy (15.7% vs 14%), both the oxidative and the glycolytic regimes of human brain activation, and an independent reconstruction; deletion of genes causing inherited brain-energy disorders compromised its energetic margin far more often than deletion of other genes (odds ratio 79, p = 6 × 10⁻²⁰). Translating the five stressors into constraints, sleep loss and cognitive load each exhausted the margin within the protocol range, at a 25% loss of mitochondrial capacity and a 39% rise in signalling demand, whereas circadian misalignment, chronic stress and reduced recovery acted on arms with reserve. Combined, the stressors exhausted the margin at 0.72 times the moderate profile; across 400 parameter draws demand was met in 99.2% at low and 28.5% at moderate exposure. Substrate oxidation, not substrate supply, set the margin: restoring sleep or reducing load restored it, whereas ketone bodies, lactate or fibre-derived acetate helped only when glucose delivery itself was limiting. Results held across thresholds, releases, solvers and enzyme-capacity limits, and the thresholds are testable with ³¹P and ¹³C spectroscopy.

In real-world consumer usage, common inflammatory conditions (e.g., acne/rosacea, (n = 708,356)) accounted for the largest share of assessments, while preventable image-acquisition errors (poor lighting: 42.0%; poor focus: 28.0%; motion blur: 18.0%) represented the primary modifiable determinants of failure. record.abstract_text: Abstract Predicting whether a pull request (PR) will be merged, rejected, or left unre solved is a recurring problem in empirical software engineering, yet it remains unclear how much explicit fusion of code changes and reviewer comments adds over simpler designs, and conclusions drawn from a single training run can be misleading. record.abstract_text: Abstract Background Skin cancer incidence is rising globally, increasing pressure on dermatology services and making efficient triage increasingly important. AI-driven skin cancer mobile health apps may help address this need, but their usefulness depends on whether users trust the advice and intend to follow it. Teledermatologist supervision has been proposed to combine AI efficiency with human clinical oversight, but dermatologist shortages make it critical to understand whether such supervision improves patient trust and adherence at the population level, or whether AI-only advice suffices for most users. Objective This study tests whether teledermatologist supervision in an AI-driven skin cancer app affects patient trust and adherence intentions, compared with AI-only advice, and whether these effects differ by motivational context and risk assessment level. Methods The randomized controlled, online vignette experiment with repeated measures was conducted from May to June 2025 as a single-center study among Dutch adults via an academic hospital-based patient panel. Eligible participants were adult members of the Erasmus MC Digital Patient Panel invited by email; those not completing all 4 vignette trials were excluded from the analysis. Participants completed 4 simulated mobile app scenarios varying in advice source (AI-only vs hybrid teledermatologist and AI) and risk assessment level (high vs low). The primary outcomes were trust in the advice (0‐100 scale) and adherence intention (recoded 3-level ordinal scale). Mixed-effects models were used to analyze the data. Results Of the 2707 patient panel members, 879 participated (response rate: 32.5%). Participants were aged 18 to 93 (mean 62.5, SD 12.64) years; 50.4% (n=443) were female, and 21.4% (n=188) had a history of skin cancer. Participants were randomly allocated to motivation conditions (concern: n=438 vs curiosity: n=441). Trust was higher for hybrid advice than AI-only advice (mean 76.9, SE 0.73 vs mean 65.7, SE 0.73; estimated difference 11.98; partial η ²=0.22; P <.001). The odds of adherence were 1.7 times greater with hybrid vs AI-only (odds ratio 1/0.59=1.7, 95% CI 1.28-2.22; P <.001). High-risk assessments increased adherence (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 2.2-3.8; P <.001), with a moderated effect by motivation ( P =.03), showing stronger adherence with concern vs curiosity. The effect of advice source on adherence was fully mediated by trust. Conclusions Teledermatologist supervision of AI-based advice robustly increased patient trust and adherence intentions, particularly for high-risk assessments and concerned users. Our experiment is innovative in testing teledermatologist supervision in a population-level AI skin cancer app and in examining how motivational context shapes responses to advice. Unlike studies focused on postreferral teledermatology or chatbot-based advice, this study isolates the effect of hybrid AI-human advice in a store-and-forward screening context. These findings suggest that developers and health care implementers may consider integrating teledermatologist supervision to maximize patient trust of and adherence to advice, potentially improving triaging efficiency and safety.

record.abstract_text: The article examines the methodological potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted acoustic analysis for investigating prosody in legal discourse. Prosody is viewed as an essential component of spoken legal communication, shaping the expression of epistemic stance, interpersonal relations, discourse organisation, and persuasive strategies through variations in pitch, intensity, rhythm, pausing, speech rate, and voice quality. The study addresses the limited attention paid to the acoustic dimension of legal discourse and evaluates the opportunities and challenges of integrating AI technologies into prosodic research. The object of the study is the prosodic organisation of spoken legal discourse; the subject is the methodological potential and limitations of AI-assisted acoustic analysis of legal speech. The aim of the study is to provide a criteria-based evaluation of AI-assisted acoustic analysis as a methodological framework for research on legal prosody. The research is theoretical and methodological, drawing on studies in acoustic phonetics, computational paralinguistics, forensic phonetics, legal linguistics, and speech processing. Descriptive, comparative, and criticalevaluative methods are applied to assess AI-assisted acoustic analysis according to six methodological criteria: validity, reliability, scalability, interpretability, ecological validity, and legal and ethical admissibility. The findings demonstrate that AI significantly improves the efficiency, reproducibility, and scalability of acoustic analysis by automating speech preprocessing, feature extraction, and computational modelling, enabling large-scale investigation of authentic legal speech. At the same time, important limitations remain, including reduced ecological validity, limited model transparency, algorithmic bias, risks of overinterpreting acoustic evidence, and legal and ethical concerns. The study argues that AI should complement rather than replace expert phonetic interpretation. It concludes that a human-in-the-loop approach integrating computational technologies with linguistic expertise provides the most reliable framework for future research on legal prosody while ensuring methodological transparency, scientific validity, and legal accountability.

record.abstract_text: The contemporary literary landscape has been fundamentally reshaped by the rise of Instapoetry: short, visual, and emotionally direct verse disseminated primarily through Instagram, a platform whose image-first architecture and recommender systems privilege affectively engaging content. This article argues that the dominance of this poetic form represents not a superficial cultural trend but an adaptive response to a digitally mediated attention economy. It advances an integrative theoretical framework explaining Instapoetry through the convergence of three dimensions: algorithmic, psychological, and cultural. First, algorithmic amplification on Instagram leverages patterns of repetition and social proof to promote specific formal styles. Second, the cognitive state of the platform’s users—marked by social media fatigue and elevated cognitive load—produces a preference for content high in processing fluency. Third, the cultural motifs that dominate Instapoetry function as accessible affective schemas, enabling readers to engage in self-expression, identity construction, and emotional validation. Drawing on research in media studies, cognitive science, and feminist literary criticism—and referencing the influential work of early Instapoets such as Rupi Kaur and Amanda Lovelace—this paper proposes a multidisciplinary account of how digital infrastructures and human psychology jointly shape contemporary poetic production and reception.

record.abstract_text: Introduction This study aims to analyse university students' perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in their academic education, exploring how they construct meaning around its use and how these representations influence notions of learning, authorship and critical literacy in higher education. Methods The sample comprised 20 students from Argentina, Chile, Mexico and Peru. The Zaltman Metaphor Elicitation Technique (ZMET) was employed as a qualitative elicitation approach using images and metaphorical narratives, applied via a two-phase protocol: a) a pre-task involving the independent selection of seven images; and b) a guided elicitation phase, based on questions that explore the participant's perception through analogies, sensory contrasts and emotional narratives. Results Within this corpus, participants articulated ambivalent representations of GenAI through several distinct metaphorical configurations, including an “other” to which participants attribute agency (a silent companion or tutor) and a pragmatic cognitive extension valued for its efficiency. These representations highlight a reconfiguration of the relationship between students and processes of knowledge production, blurring traditional boundaries between technological assistance, collaboration and authorship. On an emotional level, some accounts represented GenAI as an emotional buffer, offering relief from academic overload; however, this relief coexists with ethical vigilance and unease about “crossing a line” in academic honesty, reflecting processes of negotiation over intellectual responsibility and the legitimate use of generative systems in educational contexts. Discussion Regarding institutional adaptation, metaphors of misalignment and accounts of GenAI bridging gaps in academic support point to perceived gaps in institutional guidance and to the importance of pedagogical mediation, including clearer approaches to teaching and assessment in a context where GenAI is already part of university life. Taken together, the accounts show how participants interpret GenAI as a context-specific form of academic support and guidance. These representations link the negotiation of trust and authorship to the perceived accessibility of university support, offering insights into critical literacy and institutional mediation.

record.title: The limits of declarative authorship: the structural vulnerability of intellectual property in the age of generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Generative AI functions as a near zero cost execution engine, weakening the long standing reliance on human effort on which traditional intellectual property (IP) systems depend. The academic response has focused, so far, on studying productivity at the micro level, debating the doctrinal question of IP infringement through AI training at the macro level, or blunt denial of AI authorship. These responses miss the central problem: the human provenance at the heart of IP law is now cheap to falsify and hard to verify. In this paper I argue that AI output appropriation poses a significant threat to IP through an adverse selection dynamic. The threat comes from humans who use AI to appropriate its output and extract the value attached to human effort. Skill compression effects cutting across writing, coding, and consulting have begun to commoditize execution, compressing the quality distribution that once supported premium prices for IP protected output. This process is compounded by the difficulty of verifying declared human authorship or inventorship, which may reward deception and discourage honest effort. I therefore explore value migration from execution skill to concentrated complementary assets. Building on market evidence from platform economies, the paper considers an evolution of IP from a rights based asset model to a verification model, in which the human role shifts from creator to authenticator.

record.title: Learning-consequential assessment: making learning count when students use generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Generative AI can enable production without corresponding learning, yet wholesale exclusion from assessed work forgoes opportunities needed for workplace and lifelong learning. This article proposes learning-consequential assessment design. Students may use AI to produce assessed work, but success also depends on showing they possess the understanding their AI-supported work displays. Knowing this may encourage students to use AI for learning through explanation, comparison and challenge, rather than product optimisation alone. The central claim, that the understanding displayed is the learner's own, rests on coherence between their reasons for consequential decisions and their work, with independent performance corroborating where needed. Evidence may also warrant three capability claims: learner-directed production with AI, accountable verification of AI-shaped work and independent capability. Learning Orchestration describes the cognitive-metacognitive, epistemic and ethical judgement through which learners coordinate AI and other resources for learning, production and verification; teacher orchestration describes how teaching and assessment support its development.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: EPRA International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research (IJMR)
record.abstract_text: This study examined how internal control systems and ethical oversight shape corporate governance effectiveness in AI-driven organisations, using listed deposit money banks in Nigeria as the focus. The increasing use of artificial intelligence in banking operations has introduced governance risks that traditional control systems may no longer fully address. Previous studies mostly considered internal controls, ethics, and governance as separate issues, with limited evidence on how they work together in emerging economies. The study therefore assessed the effects of Risk Assessment, Control Activities, Information and Communication, and Monitoring Activities on Tobin’s Q, and also examined the moderating role of Ethical Oversight. A correlational and panel data research design was adopted. Secondary data were sourced from the audited annual reports and accounts of 13 listed deposit money banks in Nigeria for the period 2015 to 2024. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, Hausman specification test, and random effects regression were used for the analysis. The findings showed that all the internal control variables had positive and significant effects on Tobin’s Q, while Information and Communication had the strongest influence. Ethical Oversight also showed a positive direct effect and significantly strengthened the relationship between internal control systems and firm value. The study concludes that effective internal controls, when supported by credible ethical governance, improve market performance and broaden the traditional view of corporate governance in technology-driven institutions. It therefore recommends that deposit money banks strengthen risk management systems, widen internal audits to cover AI systems, establish active ethics committees, invest in secure digital reporting platforms, and provide continuous governance training for directors and compliance officers.

record.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, with most early applications focusing on computer-aided detection and diagnosis of lesions from endoscopic images. However, real-world endoscopic practice extends beyond image interpretation. Endoscopists must integrate real-time video, anatomical location, lesion morphology, procedural context, histopathological findings, clinical history, and standardized terminology to make diagnostic decisions and generate clinically meaningful reports. Recent advances in multimodal AI and large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to move beyond isolated endoscopic image analysis toward more comprehensive endoscopic workflow support. By integrating visual, textual, temporal, and clinical information, these models can support lesion characterization, anatomical navigation, procedure quality assessment, structured documentation, report generation, and patient-centered communication. Nevertheless, clinical translation remains limited by scarce high-quality multimodal datasets, heterogeneous reporting standards, insufficient external validation, hallucination risk, limited interpretability, real-time integration challenges, privacy concerns, and evolving regulation. This review summarizes current applications of AI in GI endoscopy, with particular emphasis on the emerging role of multimodal learning and LLMs in bridging lesion detection, context-aware interpretation, and automated report generation. Furthermore, the article analyzes future challenges and the methodological, clinical, ethical, and regulatory requirements for the reliable integration of these systems into clinical endoscopic practice.

record.title: Coping with sustainability information overload:  The role of generative artificial intelligence literacy

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: Ho Chi Minh City Open University Journal of Science - Economics and Business Administration
record.abstract_text: Consumers can use sustainability information to consume responsibly; however, excessive and complex sustainability claims might confuse consumers and hinder proper evaluations. Based on cognitive appraisal theory, this study empirically investigates the impacts of sustainability information overload (SIO) on green information avoidance (GIA) and green information verification behavior (GIVB) and examines the moderating role of generative AI literacy (GAIL) and the associations of GIA and GIVB with green purchase decision confidence (GPDC). Data from an online cross-sectional survey of 468 adult consumers in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings revealed that SIO positively influenced GIA, and GIA negatively influenced GPDC. However, SIO did not negatively influence GIVB on average. GAIL significantly moderated the SIO-GIVB relationship: SIO was negatively associated with GIVB at low GAIL but not significantly at mean or high GAIL.GIVB positively influenced GPDC. An indirect effect of SIO on GPDC through GIA is significant, but the indirect effect through GIVB is not significant unconditionally. These results suggest that sustainability information overload is associated with distinct coping responses. From a practical perspective, sustainability portals and shopping applications involving GenAI should emphasize evaluability and verifiability rather than enhancing disclosures. Through defining GAIL as a digitally mediated capability from the consumer’s perspective which can serve as a coping tool, this paper builds on cognitive appraisal theory in the context of AI-mediated sustainable consumption and explains the critical engagement of consumers with sustainability information amid overload situations.

record.title: Emotionally Aware AI Chatbots for Adolescents: A Review of Psychological Principles for Learning, Calibrated Trust, and Healthy Human–AI Interaction

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: Journal of Education, Humanities and Social Sciences
record.abstract_text: Conversational artificial intelligence now belongs to ordinary adolescent life, but the psychological research that should guide its design spreads over fields which seldom cite each other. Research on adolescent development, on misinformation susceptibility, on trust in automation, on chatbot-supported learning and on companion-chatbot overreliance has grown up separately, and each of these areas answers only part of the question of how a general-purpose chatbot should talk to a teenager. This paper brings together twenty-one sources from developmental psychology, human factors, human-computer interaction and educational technology, in order to show what is now known about adolescent chatbot interaction and what this means for conversational design. Three results appear repeatedly in this research. First, adolescence is a design context of its own, not a smaller version of adulthood, since reward sensitivity, social influence and emotional regulation are still developing, while exposure to persuasive conversational systems has already reached almost everyone. Second, trust in a chatbot changes behavior in ways that can be measured; thus, the proper design target is calibrated trust rather than maximal trust. Third, the failure modes that matter most for adolescent users, that is, hallucination, sycophancy and unwarranted confidence, originate in the model; the user is not their source. From these results this paper consolidates ten conversational design principles into four clusters, namely epistemic calibration, metacognitive scaffolding, bounded emotional support and autonomy preservation. The framework here is a conceptual synthesis and puts forward testable predictions, but it has not been empirically validated.

record.title: Rethinking English Education In The Era Of Generative Ai And Global Englishes

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: International Journal of Arts, Humanities & Social Science
record.abstract_text: The advent of generative AI has provoked an ontological crisis in language education, tempting policymakers to equate machine-generated output with human interpretive capacity. This article challenges the premise that such technologies render language learning obsolete, arguing instead that an AI-saturated landscape makes robust humanistic engagement more vital than ever. Addressing the “scholar’s dilemma,” the paper proposes a structural shift in higher education from traditional silos toward horizontal, cross-disciplinary integration. Because English functions as a global lingua franca (ELF) and exerts an algorithmic hegemony over large language models (LLMs), advanced proficiency remains indispensable for critically querying these platforms. We advocate for a pedagogical evolution from the mechanical transmission of referential information (informing) to facilitating imaginative exploration (engaging). Central to this shift is the reclamation of “literature with a small l” as the primary representational material used to cultivate students’ “textual power.” By prioritizing the interpretive struggle over cognitive offloading—a tension described here as the “Picasso Paradox”—educators can formalize a “fifth skill” (complex critical thinking in English). This framework provides the cognitive foundation for students to navigate an AI-saturated world not as passive users, but as active curators equipped with ethical discernment and epistemic agency.

record.title: Generative AI adoption in organizations: A conceptual model of job crafting, employee productivity, creativity and work engagement

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: International Journal of Business and Management (IJBM)
record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping organizational work, yet its behavioural consequences for employees remain unevenly understood. Existing research on productivity, creativity and engagement is fragmented and rarely examined within a single theoretical framework. Drawing on Job Demands Resources theory, Conservation of Resources theory and Self Determination Theory, this conceptual paper develops an integrative model of how organizational GenAI adoption affects employee productivity, creativity and work engagement. Job crafting is proposed as the central behavioural mechanism. The model treats GenAI as both a job resource and a job demand. It therefore recognizes a double edged pathway in which technology insecurity and passive over reliance can offset the benefits of adoption. AI literacy, ethical use clarity and organizational readiness are identified as boundary conditions that determine which pathway prevails. Four hypotheses are developed, covering the mediating role of job crafting for productivity and engagement, its moderating role for creativity, and the conditioning effect of AI literacy and ethical guidance. A time lagged, multi source survey design, supplemented by supervisor ratings and an optional field experiment, is proposed for future empirical testing. The paper offers a resource based account of human and AI collaboration. It also provides managerial guidance for organizations that want GenAI adoption to deliver sustainable gains in performance and well being rather than short lived efficiency gains that erode over time.

record.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Digital Marketing Strategies for Enhancing Sales Conversion in E-Commerce: An Empirical and Analytical Investigation

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: The rapid expansion of global e-commerce has intensified competition for consumer attention, rendering traditional demographic-segmented and rule-based marketing increasingly ineffective. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative paradigm in digital marketing, enabling firms to process high-velocity behavioral datasets and deliver hyper-personalized customer journeys in real time. While industry adoption of AI marketing tools is widespread, a substantial maturity gap persists between experimental deployment and fully scaled conversion optimization. This paper integrates a multi-stage analytical research design—combining psychometric Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) of consumer survey data ($N = 420$), econometric before-and-after funnel cohort modeling across retail deployments, and regression-based moderation analysis—to quantify how AI-enabled digital marketing drives sales conversion. Specifically, the study examines four core strategic pillars: neural recommendation engines, predictive programmatic acquisition, dynamic pricing optimization, and generative conversational AI. Analytical results demonstrate that Perceived Personalization significantly enhances Customer Experience Quality ($\beta = 0.499, p < 0.001$) and Digital Marketing Effectiveness ($\beta = 0.488, p < 0.001$), which jointly mediate downstream Purchase Intention and actual checkout conversion ($R^2 = 0.412$). Econometric cohort tracking further reveals a 23.4% to 31.0% relative lift in session-to-purchase conversion rates, a 27% reduction in bounce rates, and up to a 50% increase in Average Order Value (AOV) via real-time affinity bundling. However, moderation analysis confirms that perceived algorithmic opacity and privacy intrusion negatively attenuate conversion gains ($\beta = -0.214, p < 0.01$). The study concludes with an actionable governance and MLOps framework for balancing algorithmic conversion efficiency with consumer trust.

record.title: Large language model generation of plausible semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Parsons problems have been widely recognised to support novice learners by reducing the cognitive demands of writing code from scratch through rearrangement of provided code blocks. A common variation includes distractors – erroneous blocks of code which do not belong to the correct solution. While Parsons problems have been widely studied for introductory programming, they remain underexplored in various domains including in data science education, where students may possess statistical knowledge but limited programming experience. Developing distractors is also time-consuming for educators. This study investigated the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to generate semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems. A set of distractors was generated for 315 Python-based data science Parsons problems and was evaluated for pedagogical plausibility, compilability, and output divergence. Validated distractors were then incorporated as exemplars in a refined prompt to generate a second set of distractors, which were evaluated using the same criteria. The findings demonstrate that LLMs can be used to develop semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems and refining the prompts using validated exemplars further improved the quality. This study contributes to the limited literature on data science Parsons problems, distractor design and LLM-supported development of these problems.

record.title: Beyond conversation length: Conversation openings, cognitive engagement, and support orientations in student-AI chatbot interactions

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Generative AI is increasingly used in learning environments, yet sustained interaction does not necessarily indicate cognitively engaged learning. This exploratory study examined how conversation openings related to cognitive engagement levels and the support orientations reflected in student messages during student-AI interactions. Cognitive engagement was classified by an adapted ICAP framework, openings were organised into a descriptive typology, and semantic thematic analysis was conducted on student messages. Openings oriented towards strategy guidance, conceptual explanation, error understanding, and resource review feedback were more often associated with moderate or deep engagement, whereas resource-evaluation openings were often associated with longer interactions despite limited cognitive depth. Semantic patterns revealed overlapping orientations towards questioning, improvement, examples, feedback, and concepts, spanning clarification, answer checking, revision, application, and task-focused support. These findings distinguish interaction persistence from cognitive engagement and suggest that conversation design should support students to articulate their reasoning and co-construct knowledge with AI, rather than prioritising continued interaction alone.

record.title: Personalized AI-Supported Sport and Physical Activity for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Narrative Review and Conceptual Framework

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: International Journal of Sports Science and Human Performance
record.abstract_text: Background: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) show frequent motor difficulties, lower physical activity (PA) and fewer opportunities for sport participation than their peers. Individualized programs are therefore needed. Artificial intelligence (AI), wearable sensors and the Internet of Things (IoT) could support such personalization, but the evidence base has not been examined from a sport-science perspective. Objective: To synthesize evidence on PA interventions and AI- and IoT-enabled technologies relevant to children with ASD and to propose a framework for personalized, AI-supported sport and PA programs. Methods: A narrative review, guided by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA), combined a previously completed thematic synthesis of 49 studies of AI- and IoT-enabled assistive systems for children with disabilities (16 ASD-related) with targeted searches of PubMed/MEDLINE and publisher databases up to November 2026. Results: Meta-analyses indicate moderate benefits of PA interventions for motor skills, skill-related fitness and social functioning (e.g., Hedges' g = 0.62), although study quality is generally low. ASD-focused AI research mainly addresses gesture recognition, emotion analysis and socially assistive robotics in small samples (about 10–24 children), and none has tested fitness outcomes. The proposed artificial intelligence of things (AIoT)-CARE framework (Capability, Applicability, Robustness, and Ethics and Safety) links five stages: co-designed profiling, an accessible activity catalog, consent-based sensing, explainable recommendations with human override, and family-involved review. Conclusion: AI-supported personalization is a promising design direction, not a proven intervention. Phased evaluation using participant-level validation, real-world testing and AI-specific reporting guidelines is required.
